food.text: In 1952, the first espresso machines began to appear in Australia, and Italian coffee houses were emerging in Melbourne and Sydney. Pellegrini's Espresso Bar and Legend Café often claim to be Melbourne's first 'real' espresso bars, opening in 1954 and 1956.
Australian cuisine was transformed after the war by immigration programs. Migrants from the Mediterranean, East Asia and South Asia led to a large-scale diversification of local food.

For most of the twentieth century, New Zealand cuisine remained highly derivative of British food. Unlike Britain, New Zealand escaped major food shortages in World War II, though meat and butter were rationed between 1943 and 1950 because of US forces in the Pacific and exports to Britain.
The 1970s brought major changes to New Zealand take-away food with the arrival of American fast-food chains. Kentucky Fried Chicken came in 1971, Pizza Hut in 1974, and McDonald's in 1976.

Cheap air travel from about the 1960s let many New Zealanders go to Europe on overseas experience. There they met French and Italian cooking and Britain's Indian and Chinese restaurants. Back home, they created demand for better-quality food and experimented with hāngī.

The dim sim, or 'dimmy', was developed by Chinese chef William Wing Young around 1945 in Melbourne. It is a dumpling with a thick skin filled with meat and usually fried. It is often mistaken for dim sum, which is served in small baskets and steamed.

Arguably the first Modern Australian restaurant was Sydney's Bayswater Brasserie, established in 1982. It offered Mediterranean dishes with Asian and Middle Eastern influences. The term itself first appeared in print in the 1993 Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide, which placed 34 restaurants under the heading.

From 1947 into the 1950s, black rot began to hit kūmara crops in New Zealand's northern North Island. Chinese New Zealand gardeners Fay Gock and Joe Gock developed a disease-resistant variety from a mutant form of waina at their market garden in Māngere. Released commercially in 1954 as Owairaka Red, it was donated to farms in the 1960s and saved the crop.

When the United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community in 1973, it sounded the death knell of New Zealand's identity as an agricultural producer for the British Isles. Cultural ties, including cuisine, began to dilute, and dishes such as beef bourguignon entered mainstream New Zealand cooking.

Honey chilli chicken was popularised by the Australian Women's Weekly Chinese Cooking Class cookbook, originally published in 1978. Australian Chinese cuisine adapted dishes to local tastes, adding deep-fried and saucy dishes such as sweet and sour pork and sticky lemon chicken.
Vittoria, one of Australia's most iconic coffee brands, has existed in Australia since 1958, well before it moved to the US. It remains the country's largest coffee maker and distributor.

In 2020, 1,600 hectares of New Zealand land were planted in kūmara, producing 24,000 tonnes annually, mostly in Northland. Owairaka Red is the most common of the three main varieties. Toka Toka Gold was made commercially available in 1972 and is named after the Tokatoka peak near Dargaville.

Georgie Pie, a fast-food chain based on pies, was founded in New Zealand in 1977. It ran into financial trouble and went out of business in 1998, with McDonald's New Zealand buying its assets. The chain was revived in limited form between 2013 and 2020, with pies sold through McDonald's restaurants.

art.text: Contemporary Indigenous Australian art is generally regarded as beginning in 1971 with a painting movement at Papunya, northwest of Alice Springs. It involved Aboriginal artists such as Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri and Kaapa Tjampitjinpa, and was facilitated by teacher Geoffrey Bardon.

The Archibald Prize was first awarded in 1921, when William McInnes won it for his portrait of the architect Desbrowe Annear. The Art Gallery of New South Wales also awarded the inaugural Sulman Prize in 1936 to Henry Hanke for La Gitana.
art.source_title: Art Gallery of New South Wales

art.text: The Papunya movement sparked wide interest in making art across rural and remote Aboriginal Australia. Indigenous art centres helped the movement grow, and as of 2010 they were estimated to represent over 5000 artists, mostly in Australia's north and west.

The Art Gallery of New South Wales had no Indigenous Australian art until the middle of the twentieth century. In 1959, a series of 17 Pukamani grave posts from the Tiwi Islands was installed in its forecourt, which began to change public perception of Aboriginal art as contemporary art.
art.source_title: Art Gallery of New South Wales
tags: Art Gallery of New South Wales

art.text: The Brewarrina Aboriginal Cultural Museum opened in 1988 beside the ancient fish traps on the Barwon River. Its free-form building is a series of earth-covered domes representing traditional shelters called gunyas, and it won an Australian Institute of Architects award for regional architecture in 1991.
Australian cities placed building height limits early in the 20th century, typically 150 feet (45 m). These limits hampered American-style skyscrapers until they were lifted in the late 1950s.

Art + Australia is the country's longest-running art journal. It succeeded Art in Australia in 1963, and Mervyn Horton was its founding editor from 1963 to 1983. In August 2022 it became digital-only.

Indigenous art was only a minor part of the National Gallery of Australia's collection when its building opened in 1982. Early major showings came at the Sydney Biennales of 1979 and 1982, and a large-scale sand painting featured in the 1981 Sydney Festival.

Indigenous artists have won many of Australia's top art prizes. Shirley Purdie won the 2007 Blake Prize for Religious Art with Stations of the Cross, and Gloria Petyarre won the Wynne Prize in 1999 with Leaves.
The first modern blockbuster at the Art Gallery of New South Wales was Modern Masters: Monet to Matisse in 1975. It drew 180,000 people over 29 days.
art.source_title: Art Gallery of New South Wales
tags: Art Gallery of New South Wales

art.text: In November 2019 it was announced that James and Diana Ramsay had left A$38 million to the Art Gallery of South Australia to buy major works. It was one of the largest bequests ever made to an art gallery in Australia. Diana Ramsay had launched the Ramsay Art Prize in 2016.

The Art Gallery of South Australia hosts Tarnanthi, a festival of contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art held biennially. In 2018 Rhana Devenport became the gallery's first female director, after leaving the Auckland Art Gallery.

war.text: Australia entered World War II on 3 September 1939, and by the end of the war almost one million Australians had served in the armed forces. Australia also came under direct attack for the first time in its post-colonial history. Its casualties from enemy action were 27,073 killed and 23,477 wounded, and many more suffered from tropical disease, hunger and harsh conditions in captivity.

The Australians and New Zealanders, grouped together as the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC), went ashore on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April 1915. For the next eight months the Anzacs fought a costly and ultimately unsuccessful campaign against the Turks. A bloody stalemate developed at Anzac, and it is estimated there were 26,111 Australian casualties, with 8,141 killed, from combat and also from widespread disease caused by poor sanitation and hygiene in the front lines.

Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War began with 30 military advisors in 1962 and peaked at 7,672 personnel after the April 1965 decision to upgrade its commitment. By the time the last personnel were withdrawn in 1972, it had become Australia's longest war, later surpassed by the War in Afghanistan.

The Australian frontier wars were violent conflicts between Indigenous Australians and mostly British settlers, in which tens of thousands more Indigenous Australians died than Europeans. The first took place several months after the First Fleet landed in January 1788, and the last occurred in the early 20th century, some as late as 1934. Disease, famine, displacement and violence cut the Indigenous population from an estimated 300,000 to 3 million in 1788 to about 90,000 in 1901, and estimates of how many were killed in the fighting vary considerably.

Australian forces were deployed in the first campaign of World War I in German New Guinea. A hastily raised force, the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force, was dispatched in September 1914 and seized and held German possessions in the Pacific.
tags: Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force

war.text: The Japanese navy sent submarines to attack shipping off the Australian east coast, beginning with an unsuccessful midget submarine raid on Sydney Harbour on the night of 31 May 1942. Japanese submarines sank eight merchant ships by August 1942 and a further 15 in 1943. The hospital ship Centaur was torpedoed off Queensland on 14 May 1943 with the loss of 268 lives.

About 60,000 Australians served in South Vietnam between 1962 and 1972; 521 were killed and more than 3,000 were wounded. Of the 15,381 conscripted national servicemen who served from 1965 to 1972, 202 were killed and 1,279 wounded. Six Australians were listed as missing in action and are counted among the killed; the last of their remains were not located and returned to Australia until 2009.

The AIF departed Australia in November 1914 and arrived in Egypt after delays caused by German naval vessels in the Indian Ocean. There it was initially used to defend the Suez Canal, before the decision in early 1915 to land at Gallipoli.

Of the 21,467 Australian prisoners taken by the Japanese in World War II, only 14,000 survived, so roughly 7,500 did not. Many more suffered from tropical disease, hunger and harsh conditions. Throughout the fighting in Papua, most of the Australian personnel captured by Japanese troops were murdered.

More than 100 Australian airmen fought with the RAF during the Battle of Britain in 1940, including over 30 fighter pilots. Two AIF brigades, the 18th and 25th, were also stationed in Britain from June 1940 to January 1941 as part of the British mobile reserve.

At least 31 Indigenous men were killed by police in the Coniston massacre in 1928, and further reprisal expeditions were conducted in 1932 and 1933. The final frontier battles took place in the Northern Territory, where the fighting was driven by reprisals against European deaths and by pastoralists' desire to secure land that, in the article's words, they had stolen from Indigenous people.

A single German submarine, U-862, operated in the Pacific during the war. It cruised off the Australian coast and New Zealand in December 1944 and January 1945, sank two ships in Australian waters, and then returned to Batavia.

literature.text: David Unaipon was the first Aboriginal author to be published, in 1924–5. His Legendary Tales of the Australian Aborigines gave the first written accounts of Aboriginal mythology by an Aboriginal person.
Oodgeroo Noonuccal (1920–1993) was a poet, writer and rights activist. She is credited with publishing the first book of verse by an Aboriginal author, We Are Going, in 1964.

Indigenous Australian literature flourished from the 1970s through the 1990s, alongside political advocacy and a focus on land rights. Sally Morgan's 1987 memoir My Place brought Indigenous stories to wider notice.

For most of the 20th century, literature discussing homosexuality was tightly restricted by censorship in Australia. After the Book Censorship Board was established in 1933, restrictions on such books were strictly enforced, sometimes with the risk of criminal prosecution.
Peter Carey has won the Miles Franklin Award three times and the Booker Prize twice. His Booker wins were for Oscar and Lucinda in 1988 and True History of the Kelly Gang in 2001.

David Unaipon, known as the first Aboriginal author, provided the first written accounts of Aboriginal mythology by an Aboriginal person in Legendary Tales of the Aborigines (1924-1925). Oodgeroo Noonuccal later published the first book of verse by an Aboriginal author, We Are Going, in 1964.
Kim Scott was joint winner of the Miles Franklin Award with Thea Astley in 2000 for Benang, and won again in 2011 for That Deadman Dance. Alexis Wright won the award in 2007 for Carpentaria.

In 1987 Magabala Books, an Indigenous-owned enterprise, published its first book. In 1988 the University of Queensland Press established the David Unaipon Award to reward and encourage new Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers.

Jagardoo: Poems from Aboriginal Australia, published in 1978, was the second poetry collection by Noongar playwright and poet Jack Davis. He is often referred to as the 20th century's Aboriginal Poet Laureate.
No End to the Way, written by G. M. Glaskin under the pseudonym Neville Jackson, was banned from 1965 to 1966. It is generally regarded as the first openly homosexual Australian novel.

The Monkey's Mask by Dorothy Porter, published in 1994, is a crime novel in verse about a queer detective in the dangerous streets of Sydney. It has been adapted for radio, television and film, and published in multiple languages.

Seaforth Mackenzie's The Young Desire It, published in the UK in 1937, was a rare exception: it was allowed into Australia even though the Book Censorship Board considered it to contain homosexual content. It won the 1937 Australian Literature Society Gold Medal.

science.text: Science & Technology Australia is the country's peak body for science and technology. It represents more than 90,000 Australian scientists and technologists working across all scientific disciplines. It was known as the Federation of Australian Scientific and Technological Societies until June 2011.
tags: Federation of Australian Scientific and Technological Societies

science.text: Australia has five learned academies: Humanities, Science, Technological Sciences and Engineering, Health and Medical Sciences, and the Social Sciences. They cooperate through the Australian Council of Learned Academies, which was formed in 1995.
science.source_title: Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia
tags: Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia

science.text: The Federation of Australian Scientific and Technological Societies was formed in late 1985. It was a reaction to the 1984 Australian Federal Budget, which made substantial cuts to science funding. Its formation followed Science Minister Barry Jones saying the science community had not given him enough support in dealings with cabinet.
tags: Federation of Australian Scientific and Technological Societies

science.text: The Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia was incorporated on 7 July 1971. Its 96 Council members became its first Fellows. Today it has an elected Fellowship of over 750 researchers and professionals who advise governments on issues of national importance.
science.source_title: Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia
tags: Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia
Social Science Research Council of Australia

science.text: In 2017, Science & Technology Australia created Superstars of STEM, a program meant to provide role models for women and non-binary people in science, technology, engineering and maths. It gives participants media and science communications training, so they can appear as experts in the media, on stage and in schools.

The path to the Academy of the Social Sciences began in 1942, when members of the Australian National Research Council proposed a Social Science Research Council. In 1943 the Council set up a Social Science Research Committee, and in 1952 that committee resolved to become an autonomous body. The Academy itself followed in 1971.
science.source_title: Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia
tags: Social Science Research Council of Australia
Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia

politics.text: Australia entered World War II on 3 September 1939, following the government's acceptance of the United Kingdom's declaration of war on Nazi Germany. It later declared war on Italy on 11 June 1940 and on Japan on 9 December 1941. By the war's end almost one million Australians had served in the armed forces, and 27,073 had been killed and 23,477 wounded by enemy action. Many more suffered from tropical disease, hunger and harsh conditions in captivity; of the 21,467 Australian prisoners taken by the Japanese, only 14,000 survived.

Holt won the 1967 election with the largest parliamentary majority in 65 years. He drowned while swimming at a surf beach in December 1967, and John Gorton replaced him as leader. Gorton's government began winding down Australia's commitment to Vietnam.

The Science Party was established on 2 July 2013 under the name Future Party. Its founding leader, James Jansson, was studying for his doctorate at the Kirby Institute at the time. The party aimed to advance Australian society through technical and long-term solutions.

The Statute of Westminster 1931 ended the ability of the UK to legislate for Australia at the federal level without Australia's consent. Australia adopted it only in 1942, but the adoption was backdated to 1939 to confirm the validity of legislation passed during World War II.

After Gorton, the Liberals turned to William McMahon, who led from 1971 to 1972. He faced a reinvigorated Australian Labor Party under Gough Whitlam. The Liberals then entered the final stretch of a record 23 straight years in office.
Australia was a founding member of the League of Nations in 1920, and of the United Nations in 1945. Since 1901 it had been a self-governing dominion within the British Empire.

The 1960s and 1970s brought landmark laws in South Australia. The 1966 Prohibition of Discrimination Act banned discrimination on grounds of race, colour or country of origin. In 1975 the Sex Discrimination Act made discrimination on grounds of gender, marital status or sexuality unlawful.

The Aborigines Act Amendment Act 1939 abolished South Australia's office of Chief Protector of Aborigines and the Advisory Council of Aborigines. It created the Aborigines Protection Board, of which Charles Duguid was a founding member.

As of January 2020, six Indigenous Australians had been elected to the Australian Senate. The first was Neville Bonner, a Liberal who served from 1971 to 1983. Later members include Aden Ridgeway, Nova Peris, Jacqui Lambie, Pat Dodson and Malarndirri McCarthy.

The history wars were public disputes between about 1993 and 2007 involving historians, politicians and media commentators over how to interpret Australian history. They grew out of the revisionist histories of the 1970s and debates about multiculturalism, Indigenous land rights, the stolen generations and national identity. The 1997 Bringing Them Home report on the forced removal of Indigenous children from their families said the policy amounted to genocide, and in 2002 Keith Windschuttle argued that there had been no genocide of Aboriginal Tasmanians and that historians had misrepresented the violence against them, which set off bitter debate about settler violence against Aboriginal people.

The Future Party changed its name to The Science Party on 22 March 2016, after registering with the Australian Electoral Commission. It ran candidates in the 2013, 2016 and 2019 federal elections. On 12 January 2022 it was de-registered for failing to meet the new requirement of 1,500 members, and it later merged into the Fusion Party.

In South Australia, the Aborigines' Office became the Aborigines' Department in 1912, at first a change in name only. In 1918 an Advisory Council of Aborigines was appointed under the Aborigines Act 1911 to take control of the existing missions at Point McLeay, Point Pearce, Killalpaninna and Koonibba.

The Science Party fielded Meow-Ludo Meow-Meow in the 2017 New England by-election. The party chose him in response to the 2017–2018 Australian parliamentary eligibility crisis. He had earlier been its candidate in the Division of Grayndler at the 2016 federal election.

philosophy.text: Australian realism was a school of philosophy that flourished in the first half of the 20th century at several Australian universities. Its central claim, stated by John Anderson, was that whatever exists is real, on the same level of reality as anything else that exists.

Australian academic philosophy has mostly been pursued in universities and has broadly followed the Anglo-American analytic tradition. It has also included idealism, Catholic neo-scholasticism, Marxism, and continental, feminist and Asian philosophy.

Australian realism began after John Anderson accepted the Challis Chair of Philosophy at the University of Sydney in 1927. His students included John Passmore, J. L. Mackie, David Stove, Eugene Kamenka and David Malet Armstrong.

John Anderson held that a correct view of the world meant rejecting any sort of deity. It also meant rejecting the extraordinary entities postulated by many philosophers from at least the time of Plato onward.

Anderson's controversial atheism and his view that there was no such thing as moral obligation attracted condemnation. Through his students, he influenced the Sydney Push and other libertarian currents of the 1960s.

In Adelaide during the 1950s, the mind-brain identity theory was developed independently of the Andersonians. Its authors were J. J. C. Smart, then Chair of Philosophy at the University of Adelaide, and Ullin Place, both former students of Gilbert Ryle.

John Anderson's promotion of atheism was continued by John Mackie in his 1981 book The Miracle of Theism. More recently, Graham Oppy has defended atheism in books such as Atheism: The Basics, published in 2018.

Some Australian philosophers developed non-standard views of God, such as Samuel Alexander in Space, Time and Deity, published in 1920. Peter Forrest later did so in Developmental Theism, published in 2007.
Graham Nerlich argued in The Shape of Space, published in 1976, that space is not merely relational properties of distance. In his view, space is a real entity in itself.
The philosophy of religion journal Sophia was founded by Max Charlesworth in Melbourne in 1962. It has published widely on Eastern as well as Western approaches to religion.

James Franklin and the Sydney School developed the Anderson-Armstrong one level of reality view into a philosophy of mathematics. It is opposed to both Platonism and nominalism, and holds that mathematics studies properties such as symmetry, continuity and order that can be realized in the physical world.

culture.text: In the 2021 national census, 43.9% of Australians identified with Christianity and 38.9% declared "no religion". Christianity was at 88% in the 1966 census and 96% in the 1911 census, while "no religion" stood at 15.5% in 2001.

A coffee culture grew in Australia from independent cafes, and it flourished first in Leichhardt, Sydney, which had a high concentration of Italian immigrants. Australians are more focused on specialty coffee, including sourcing fresh beans and roasting properly, and Starbucks had a very low market share there in 2018.
In 2000, Aboriginal sprinter Cathy Freeman lit the Olympic flame at the opening ceremony of the Summer Olympics in Sydney. She went on to win the 400 metres at the Games.

Australia is one of five nations to have participated in every Summer Olympics of the modern era. It hosted the Games in Melbourne in 1956 and Sydney in 2000, and is set to host the 2032 Games in Brisbane.

The Australians and New Zealanders, grouped together as the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC), went ashore at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915 and fought a costly and ultimately unsuccessful eight-month campaign against the Turks. It ended in disastrous failure: an estimated 26,111 Australian casualties, with 8,141 killed, from combat and also from widespread disease caused by poor sanitation and hygiene in the front lines. For Australians, the war and the Gallipoli campaign became a symbol of the nation's emergence as an international actor, and many notions of Australian character and nationhood have their origins in it.

In 1952, the first espresso machines began to appear in Australia. Pellegrini's Espresso Bar and Legend Café both lay claim to being Melbourne's first "real" espresso bar, opening in 1954 and 1956 respectively.

In 1973, Arthur Beetson became the first Indigenous Australian to captain his country in any sport, leading the Kangaroos rugby league team. In 1982, Mark Ella became captain of the Australia national rugby union team.

The flat white has been described by The Economist as Australia's greatest culinary export. Café owner Alan Preston claims he used the term "flat white" for the menu of Sydney's Moors Espresso Bar in 1985, though the drink's origins are contested.
In 1971, the census instruction "if no religion, write none" was introduced. This saw a sevenfold increase from the previous census year in the percentage of Australians stating they had no religion.
